catalog_quote: With the exception of a handful of words, stress is predictable in Tsou. As was seen in the examples above, stress tends to fall on the penultimate syllable. ... This, however, is not the full story. When a word ends in a long vowel, stress falls on the last syllable. ... The full generalization, then, is that stress falls on the final syllable if it has a long vowel, else on the penultimate syllable. This pattern is one of Tung's motivations for describing long vowels as disyllabic; he wanted to say that stress was always on the penultimate syllable. Tung, however, was writing before the advent of metrical theories of stress such as that described in detail in Hayes (1993) and thus lacked the tools for analyzing this pattern as moraic stress. new_statements.quote: p. 218: "Stress regularly falls on the penultimate syllable in Duhtu, e.g., rápta 'bark (of tree),' bə́vnə 'flower,' moriʔhóca 'lightning.' The regularity of stress is preserved in so far as stress automatically shifts its position to the penult when a sound change (such as from a consonant to a vowel z > i) occurs in the last two syllables, e.g., Duhtu tahíza, Tfuea táhza, Tapangu tahía 'beans;' ... The regularity of stress can generally be maintained if a phonemic contrast between a semiconsonant and vowel is set up in Tapangu and Tfuea. Or else the sound change r > e may disrupt the stress pattern." p. 219: "While stress is still on the penult in I, it shifts to the antepenut [sic] in II, which destroys the regular pattern of stress." p. 224: "The form /fʔɨ́r/ 'sweet potato' as transcribed by Tung appears to allow a consonant in the final position and stress in the final syllable, the only exceptions in the distribution."

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog record (Wright & Ladefoged 1994: penultimate stress, final if the word ends in a long vowel; W&L themselves note that Tung, Li and Ho treat long vowels as two syllables so that stress is uniformly penultimate). Li 1979 states the penultimate regularity in segmental (Tung-style) terms, adds the dialect scope (Duhtu explicitly; Tapangu/Tfuea via the transcription argument), the automatic stress shift under z > i, the dependence of 'regular penult' on analysing post-vocalic e (< *r) as a semiconsonant, and disposes of Tung's single final-stress form. It says nothing about long vowels attracting final stress, so it neither confirms nor denies the weight clause; no co…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is regular (non-contrastive) on the penultimate syllable; stated explicitly for the Duhtu dialect and treated as the regular pattern of Tsou generally: when a sound change alters the syllable count of the last two syllables (z > i), stress moves so as to stay penultimate (Duhtu tahíza ~ Tfuea táhza ~ Tapangu tahía). In Tapangu and Tfuea the reflex of *r written as a semiconsonant y (column I) keeps stress penultimate; writing it as a vowel e (column II, phonetically closer) makes a good number of forms surface with antepenultimate stress (kóeu, náveu, póezi, tʔóeŋa..), which Li flags as a transcription problem rather than a different stress rule. Tung's Duhtu /fʔɨ́r/ 'sweet potato' would be the only final-stressed, consonant-final form; Li retranscribes it fʔúre, removing the exception.
new_statements.exceptions: Apparent antepenultimate stress in Tapangu/Tfuea forms where *r > e is written as a vowel (List IV items 14, 17, 18, 29, 35, 45, 54, 56, 64, 66, 68 and kóeu, náveu, símeo, póei/póezi, ŋáeo, tʔóeŋa, sváeə, ezóeə); Tung's final-stressed /fʔɨ́r/ 'sweet potato' (re-heard by Li as [re], i.e. penultimate). Long vowels / final heavy syllables are not discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: Li 1979 treats all three extant Tsou dialects (Tapangu, Tfuea, Duhtu; Iimucu extinct) from his 1978 fieldwork in Tapangu and Mamahavana (Duhtu) villages; the explicit stress statement is made for Duhtu (based on the last /r/-preserving speaker, Avai Tenayana, 74) and extended to Tapangu/Tfuea through the transcription discussion. The catalog's Wright & Ladefoged 1994 record is based on Tfuya (Tfuea) speakers.

(2) Deciding source: a 1994 instrumental phonetic study whose stress section is a descriptive restatement and moraic reanalysis of Tung 1964's data, not a measurement; the facts are independently corroborated by the held Chang & Pan 2016 CIP grammar (fixed penultimate syllable / penultimate vowel, long vowels as sequences, stress shifts under suffixation: peísu -> peisú’u), which is exactly the Tung-style analysis already recorded in the secondary-stress rule. No source seen disagrees on the surface pattern; the 'weight (CVV)' vs 'fixed penult by vowel count' label is an analytic equivalence the record documents. sources.note: Translation: 'Stress usually falls on the penultimate syllable of the word, e.g. amo father, tacʉmʉ banana, bochio know. After suffixation the stress still falls on the penultimate syllable of the word, e.g. amo-'u my father, tacʉmʉ-su your banana, cohiv-i know.' p. 82 adds that bound pronouns count as suffixes because stress stays on the penult of the new word (ino ~ ino-'u, tena ~ tena-ta).
